stem: Hale sues Brightway Movers for negligence after a Brightway truck struck Hale's car. Brightway holds a liability policy under which its insurer may be liable to satisfy part or all of a judgment. The parties have just held their Rule 26(f) conference. Hale has served no discovery request, and no stipulation or court order changes the usual disclosure rules.
ask: What must Brightway do about the policy?

options.t: Make it available to Hale for inspection and copying as an initial disclosure, without waiting for a request.
options.why: Rule 26(a)(1)(A)(iv) requires each party, without awaiting a discovery request, to make an insurance agreement that may satisfy a judgment available for inspection and copying.

options.t: Do nothing until Hale serves a Rule 34 request, because initial disclosures reach only material Brightway plans to use.
options.why: The 'may use' limit appears in Rule 26(a)(1)(A)(i) and (ii), not (iv), and disclosure is due 'without awaiting a discovery request.'

options.t: Describe the policy by category and location, without making the agreement itself available.
options.why: A category-and-location description is the option in Rule 26(a)(1)(A)(ii) for documents; (iv) requires the agreement itself for inspection and copying.

options.t: Disclose it only if the court orders disclosure after Hale shows good cause.
options.why: Adds a requirement the rule lacks; Rule 26(a)(1)(A) disclosures are automatic and need no order or showing.

explain: Rule 26(a)(1)(A)(iv) requires a party, without awaiting a discovery request, to provide any insurance agreement under which an insurer may be liable to satisfy all or part of a judgment, for inspection and copying. Brightway's liability policy fits. The 'may use' and 'category and location' language belongs to subparagraphs (i) and (ii), and no order or showing is needed.

cites.quote: for inspection and copying as under Rule 34, any insurance agreement under which an insurance business may be liable to satisfy all or part of a possible judgment in the action or to indemnify or reimburse for payments made to satisfy the judgment
without awaiting a discovery request

stem: Nash sues Tern Co. and Vale Co. The parties hold their Rule 26(f) conference on Tuesday, March 3, 2026. Nash then amends the complaint to add Lowell Inc. as a defendant, and Lowell is first served with process on Monday, April 6, 2026. No stipulation or court order sets a different time for initial disclosures, and the case is not exempt from them.
ask: By what date must Lowell make its initial disclosures?

options.t: April 20, 2026
options.why: Uses the 14-day period of Rule 26(a)(1)(C), which runs from the conference and applies to parties who were present at it, not to a party first served later.

options.t: March 17, 2026
options.why: Measures 14 days from the March 3 conference, but Lowell was not yet a party; Rule 26(a)(1)(D) governs a party first served after the conference.

options.t: June 5, 2026
options.why: Uses a 60-day period that appears nowhere in Rule 26(a)(1).
Lowell was first served after the Rule 26(f) conference, so Rule 26(a)(1)(D) gives it 30 days after being served; day 30 after April 6 is Wednesday, May 6.

explain: Lowell is a party first served after the Rule 26(f) conference, so Rule 26(a)(1)(D) controls, not the conference-based 14 days of Rule 26(a)(1)(C). Excluding April 6 and counting 30 days gives Wednesday, May 6, 2026, a business day. Nothing in the facts displaces the 30-day period by stipulation or order.

cites.quote: A party that is first served or otherwise joined after the Rule 26(f) conference must make the initial disclosures within 30 days after being served or joined, unless a different time is set by stipulation or court order.
at or within 14 days after the parties' Rule 26(f) conference

stem: Kerr sues Lund Bank, claiming Lund wrongly declared a default on Kerr's loan. Kerr requests a loan officer's internal memo about Kerr's account that bears directly on the claimed default. The memo is not privileged. Lund's only objection is that the memo would not be admissible at trial, so it cannot be discovered; Lund raises no proportionality objection.
ask: How should the court rule on Lund's objection?

options.t: Sustain it, because discovery is limited to matter that would be admissible at trial.
options.why: Rule 26(b)(1) states the opposite: information within the scope 'need not be admissible in evidence to be discoverable.'

options.t: Overrule it only if the memo is likely to lead to admissible evidence.
options.why: Rule 26(b)(1) contains no 'likely to lead to admissible evidence' test; the scope is relevance to a claim or defense plus proportionality.

options.t: Overrule it; information within Rule 26(b)(1)'s scope need not be admissible.
options.why: Rule 26(b)(1) says information within the scope of discovery need not be admissible in evidence to be discoverable; the memo is relevant to a claim and nonprivileged.

options.t: Sustain it unless Kerr shows substantial need and undue hardship.
options.why: That showing is the Rule 26(b)(3)(A)(ii) test for trial-preparation materials; an ordinary business memo is not one.

explain: Rule 26(b)(1) permits discovery of nonprivileged matter relevant to a party's claim or defense and proportional to the needs of the case, and adds that such information need not be admissible to be discoverable. The memo bears on the default, is not privileged, and no proportionality objection was made. Lund's admissibility objection fails.

cites.quote: Information within this scope of discovery need not be admissible in evidence to be discoverable.
any nonprivileged matter that is relevant to any party's claim or defense and proportional to the needs of the case

stem: A fire destroys a warehouse owned by Cobalt Foods. Because a suit was threatened, Cobalt's liability insurer, at the request of Cobalt's lawyer, sends an adjuster who photographs the site the next day. The site is cleared a week later. Dunn, a neighbor, sues Cobalt and requests the photographs. They are relevant to Dunn's claim. Dunn has no images of the unaltered site and no other source for equivalent ones.
ask: May Dunn obtain the photographs?

options.t: No, because only materials prepared by a party or its attorney are protected, and an insurer's adjuster is neither.
options.why: Rule 26(b)(3)(A) covers materials prepared by or for a party or its representative, expressly including an insurer.

options.t: Yes, on a showing of substantial need that Dunn cannot meet without undue hardship by other means.
options.why: The photos were prepared in anticipation of litigation for a party by its insurer, but Rule 26(b)(3)(A)(ii) allows discovery on a showing of substantial need and no substantial equivalent.

options.t: No, because materials prepared in anticipation of litigation are never discoverable.
options.why: Rule 26(b)(3)(A) says 'ordinarily' and then permits discovery on the substantial need showing.

options.t: Yes, with no showing, because photographs record facts rather than attorney opinions.
options.why: Rule 26(b)(3)(A) protects documents and tangible things; only the Rule 26(b)(3)(B) opinion protection is about mental impressions, and the (A)(ii) showing is still required.

explain: The photographs were prepared in anticipation of litigation for Cobalt by its insurer, a listed representative, so Rule 26(b)(3)(A) ordinarily bars discovery. But they are discoverable if relevant and Dunn shows substantial need and inability to obtain the substantial equivalent without undue hardship. The site is gone and no other images exist, so Dunn can make that showing.

cites.quote: by or for another party or its representative (including the other party's attorney, consultant, surety, indemnitor, insurer, or agent)
the party shows that it has substantial need for the materials to prepare its case and cannot, without undue hardship, obtain their substantial equivalent by other means

stem: In a product suit, Park designates Dr. Voss, a retained expert who will testify at trial and must provide a Rule 26(a)(2)(B) report. Delta Mills requests Voss's drafts and all emails between Park's lawyer and Voss. The emails include one fixing Voss's hourly rate, one listing three test results that counsel supplied and that Voss considered in forming her opinions, and several on how to present her testimony. No stipulation or order applies.
ask: What may Delta Mills obtain?

options.t: All the emails, but not the drafts.
options.why: Rule 26(b)(4)(C) protects the lawyer-expert communications except the three listed categories, so the presentation emails stay protected.

options.t: Only the rate email and the test-results email.
options.why: Rule 26(b)(4)(B) protects the drafts, and Rule 26(b)(4)(C) protects the lawyer-expert emails except those on compensation (i) and on facts or data counsel provided and the expert considered (ii).

options.t: Nothing, because the drafts and all lawyer-expert communications are protected.
options.why: Ignores the exceptions in Rule 26(b)(4)(C)(i)-(iii) for compensation, facts or data provided and considered, and assumptions relied on.

options.t: The drafts and the rate email, but not the test-results email.
options.why: Drafts are protected by Rule 26(b)(4)(B), and the test-results email falls within the exception in Rule 26(b)(4)(C)(ii).

explain: Voss is a report-writing expert, so Rule 26(b)(4)(B) protects her drafts and Rule 26(b)(4)(C) protects counsel's communications with her, except those relating to compensation (i), identifying facts or data counsel provided and she considered (ii), or identifying assumptions she relied on (iii). The rate email and the test-results email fit exceptions; the drafts and presentation emails do not.

cites.quote: protect drafts of any report or disclosure required under Rule 26(a)(2), regardless of the form in which the draft is recorded
relate to compensation for the expert's study or testimony
identify facts or data that the party's attorney provided and that the expert considered in forming the opinions to be expressed

stem: In discovery, Orion Freight mistakenly produces to Reed an email chain between Orion and its lawyer. On Tuesday, Orion's counsel notifies Reed in writing that the chain is privileged and states the basis. Before the notice, Reed's lawyer had forwarded the chain to Reed's retained expert. Reed doubts that the privilege claim is valid.
ask: What must Reed do now?

options.t: Return, sequester or destroy it, retrieve it from the expert, and refrain from using it.
options.why: Rule 26(b)(5)(B) imposes all of these duties on a notified party, including retrieval of information disclosed before notice, and lets Reed present it to the court under seal.

options.t: Return the chain but keep using what Reed's team learned from it, since Orion produced it voluntarily.
options.why: Rule 26(b)(5)(B) bars use or disclosure until the claim is resolved and contains no exception for voluntary production.

options.t: Nothing, unless Orion moves for a protective order within 14 days of its notice.
options.why: The duties arise on notification; Rule 26(b)(5)(B) sets no motion requirement or 14-day trigger.

options.t: Return or destroy the chain, but leave the expert's copy alone because it is outside Reed's own files.
options.why: Rule 26(b)(5)(B) requires reasonable steps to retrieve information that was disclosed before the notice.

explain: Orion's notice triggers Rule 26(b)(5)(B). Reed must promptly return, sequester, or destroy the information and its copies, must not use or disclose it until the claim is resolved, and must take reasonable steps to retrieve it from the expert, to whom it was forwarded before notice. Reed may also present it under seal to the court to test the claim.

cites.quote: must promptly return, sequester, or destroy the specified information and any copies it has; must not use or disclose the information until the claim is resolved; must take reasonable steps to retrieve the information if the party disclosed it before being notified

stem: Sable sues Quarry Inc. and serves a Rule 34 request for Quarry's customer list, which Quarry treats as a trade secret. Quarry's lawyer files a motion for a protective order in the court where the action is pending, supported by a declaration describing the competitive harm. She never contacts Sable's lawyer before filing. Sable opposes, arguing only that the motion lacks a required certification.
ask: Is Sable's objection well taken?

options.t: No; that certification is required only for a motion to compel under Rule 37(a)(1).
options.why: Rule 26(c)(1) has its own certification requirement for protective-order motions.

options.t: No; a declaration showing good cause can substitute for the certification.
options.why: Rule 26(c)(1) treats good cause as the court's standard for the order and the certification as a separate requirement of the motion.

options.t: Yes, but only because Quarry is a party; a nonparty's motion needs no certification.
options.why: Rule 26(c)(1) applies to 'a party or any person from whom discovery is sought' alike.

options.t: Yes; the motion lacked a certification of a good-faith conference or attempt.
options.why: Rule 26(c)(1) requires every motion for a protective order to include a certification that the movant conferred or tried to confer in good faith.

explain: Rule 26(c)(1) lets a party or any person from whom discovery is sought move for a protective order, but the motion must include a certification that the movant conferred or tried in good faith to confer with affected parties to resolve the dispute without court action. Quarry made no contact, so its motion is deficient. Good cause is the standard for the order, not a substitute.

cites.quote: The motion must include a certification that the movant has in good faith conferred or attempted to confer with other affected parties in an effort to resolve the dispute without court action.
A party or any person from whom discovery is sought may move for a protective order

stem: Ito sues Larch Co. for breach of contract. In answer to Ito's interrogatory asking who witnessed the delivery, Larch names two employees. Months later, with discovery still open, Larch's lawyer learns of a third witness, a truck driver, whom Ito has never been told about and who appears in no document or deposition. No stipulation or order addresses supplementation.
ask: Must Larch supplement its interrogatory answer?

options.t: No; the duty to answer ended when Larch served its answer.
options.why: Rule 26(e)(1) imposes a continuing duty on a party who has responded to an interrogatory.

options.t: Yes, but only if Ito serves a new interrogatory asking about the driver.
options.why: Rule 26(e)(1)(A) requires supplementation on the party's own learning of the gap, not on a new request.

options.t: Yes; it must correct the incomplete answer in a timely manner.
options.why: Rule 26(e)(1)(A) requires timely supplementation when a response is materially incomplete and the information was not otherwise made known to the other parties.

options.t: Yes, but not until the Rule 26(a)(3) pretrial disclosures are due.
options.why: That deadline governs additions to an expert's report or deposition information under Rule 26(e)(2); other responses must be supplemented in a timely manner.

explain: Larch responded to an interrogatory, so Rule 26(e)(1) obliges it to correct or supplement in a timely manner if it learns the response is incomplete in some material respect and the information has not otherwise been made known during discovery or in writing. The unknown third witness meets both conditions. The pretrial-disclosure deadline is limited to expert information.

cites.quote: in a timely manner if the party learns that in some material respect the disclosure or response is incomplete or incorrect, and if the additional or corrective information has not otherwise been made known to the other parties during the discovery process or in writing
Any additions or changes to this information must be disclosed by the time the party's pretrial disclosures under Rule 26(a)(3) are due.

stem: The court sets a Rule 16(b) scheduling conference for Tuesday, May 5, 2026. The action is not exempt from initial disclosure, the court has not ordered otherwise, and no local rule shortens the usual period for the parties' discovery conference.
ask: By what date, at the latest, must the parties hold their Rule 26(f) conference?

options.t: April 21, 2026
options.why: Uses 14 days, the period in Rule 26(f)(2) for submitting the written report after the conference, not the lead time before the scheduling conference.

options.t: April 7, 2026
options.why: Uses 28 days, a lead time Rule 26(f)(1) does not set.

options.t: April 14, 2026
options.why: Rule 26(f)(1) requires the conference at least 21 days before the scheduling conference; counting back 21 days from May 5 gives Tuesday, April 14.
Counts 21 days after the scheduling conference; the rule requires the conference to occur before it.

explain: Absent a court order or an expedited-schedule local rule, Rule 26(f)(1) requires the parties to confer at least 21 days before a scheduling conference is held or a scheduling order is due. Counting back 21 days from Tuesday, May 5, 2026 gives Tuesday, April 14, 2026, a business day, as the last permissible date.

cites.quote: the parties must confer as soon as practicable—and in any event at least 21 days before a scheduling conference is to be held or a scheduling order is due under Rule 16(b)
for submitting to the court within 14 days after the conference a written report outlining the plan

stem: Vega sues Orchard Bank for fraud and seeks $400,000 in lost profits. The parties have held their Rule 26(f) conference. Vega plans to use a spreadsheet of her monthly sales to support her damages claim. She also has surveillance photos of an Orchard officer that she would use only to contradict him if he testifies inconsistently. She intends to call a retained economist at trial. Vega has no insurance covering this claim. No stipulation or order changes the disclosure rules, and the action is not one of the exempt proceedings in Rule 26(a)(1)(B).
ask: Which provisions require Vega to make disclosures on these facts? Select all that apply.

options.t: Rule 26(a)(1)(A)(ii)
options.why: She may use the spreadsheet to support her claim, so she must produce it or describe it by category and location; the impeachment-only photos are excluded.

options.t: Rule 26(a)(1)(A)(iii)
options.why: She claims lost profits, so she must give a computation of each category of damages and make its supporting materials available.

options.t: Rule 26(a)(1)(A)(iv)
options.why: Vega has no insurance agreement that could satisfy a judgment, so this disclosure does not arise.

options.t: Rule 26(a)(1)(B)
options.why: The facts say the action is not an exempt proceeding, so initial disclosure is required.

options.t: Rule 26(a)(2)(B)
options.why: The economist is retained to give expert testimony, so Vega must disclose her identity with a signed written report.

options.t: Rule 26(a)(2)(C)
options.why: That subparagraph covers witnesses who need not give a written report; a retained expert must give one.

explain: The spreadsheet Vega may use triggers Rule 26(a)(1)(A)(ii), though the impeachment-only photos are excluded, and her lost-profits claim triggers the damages computation under (A)(iii). The retained economist triggers Rule 26(a)(2)(B). She has no insurance, so (A)(iv) does not apply. The action is not exempt, so (B) is no defense, and (2)(C) is for non-report witnesses.

cites.quote: all documents, electronically stored information, and tangible things that the disclosing party has in its possession, custody, or control and may use to support its claims or defenses, unless the use would be solely for impeachment
a computation of each category of damages claimed by the disclosing party
this disclosure must be accompanied by a written report—prepared and signed by the witness—if the witness is one retained or specially employed to provide expert testimony in the case

stem: Zane sues Hollis Corp. Hollis withholds three items from production and says only: 'Withheld as privileged.' The items are an email of legal advice from Hollis's general counsel, a memo Hollis's lawyer wrote after Zane threatened suit, and a witness statement that a nonparty, Cho, signed for Hollis's investigator. Cho asks Hollis for a copy of her own statement, and Hollis refuses. Hollis then moves for a protective order against a deposition topic, and the motion says nothing about any contact with Zane's lawyer. Hollis has produced nothing by mistake and has retained no experts.
ask: Which provisions of Rule 26 apply to these events? Select all that apply.

options.t: Rule 26(b)(2)(B)
options.why: No one claims that any electronically stored information is not reasonably accessible.

options.t: Rule 26(b)(3)(C)
options.why: Cho signed the statement, so on request she may obtain her own statement without the substantial-need showing.

options.t: Rule 26(b)(4)(D)
options.why: Hollis has retained no experts, so the non-testifying-expert protection is not in play.

options.t: Rule 26(b)(5)(A)
options.why: Hollis must expressly claim privilege and describe the withheld items so others can assess the claim; a bare 'withheld as privileged' does not.

options.t: Rule 26(b)(5)(B)
options.why: Nothing was produced by mistake, so no clawback notice or return duty arises.

options.t: Rule 26(c)(1)
options.why: The protective-order motion must include a certification of a good-faith conference or attempt, and this one has none.

explain: Cho may demand her own signed statement without showing need (26(b)(3)(C)). Hollis's one-line response fails to describe the withheld items enough for assessment (26(b)(5)(A)). Its protective-order motion lacks the required good-faith certification (26(c)(1)). No ESI accessibility claim, expert, or mistaken production appears, so (b)(2)(B), (b)(4)(D) and (b)(5)(B) are out.

cites.quote: Any party or other person may, on request and without the required showing, obtain the person's own previous statement about the action or its subject matter.

describe the nature of the documents, communications, or tangible things not produced or disclosed—and do so in a manner that, without revealing information itself privileged or protected, will enable other parties to assess the claim
The motion must include a certification that the movant has in good faith conferred or attempted to confer with other affected parties in an effort to resolve the dispute without court action.

stem: Before any Rule 26(f) conference in a non-exempt action, Dray serves interrogatories on Pine Co. Pine's lawyer serves responses signed only 'Pine Co. Legal Dept.,' with no attorney's name, address, e-mail or telephone number. The objections call every interrogatory 'unduly burdensome,' though the lawyer made no inquiry and chose them solely to delay the case. Pine's answers were complete and correct when served, and nothing has changed since. Pine has not asked for a protective order and has withheld nothing as privileged.
ask: Which provisions of Rule 26 bear on these events? Select all that apply.

options.t: Rule 26(b)(5)(A)
options.why: Pine withheld nothing as privileged, so no privilege description is owed.

options.t: Rule 26(c)(1)
options.why: Pine has not moved for a protective order, so the conference certification is not at issue.

options.t: Rule 26(d)(1)
options.why: Dray sought discovery before the Rule 26(f) conference in a non-exempt action, and no rule, stipulation or order authorizes it.

options.t: Rule 26(e)(1)(A)
options.why: The answers were complete and correct and nothing has changed, so there is nothing to supplement.

options.t: Rule 26(g)(1)
options.why: A response or objection must be signed by an attorney of record in the attorney's own name with address, e-mail and telephone number.

options.t: Rule 26(g)(2)
options.why: The unsigned responses need not be acted on, and the court must strike them unless a signature is promptly supplied.

options.t: Rule 26(g)(3)
options.why: Objections chosen without reasonable inquiry solely to delay violate the certification, calling for a mandatory sanction absent substantial justification.

explain: Dray's interrogatories were premature under 26(d)(1). Pine's responses lack an attorney of record's signature and contact details (26(g)(1)); under 26(g)(2) the court must strike them unless a signature is promptly supplied. Objections made without inquiry and solely to delay violate the certification and require a sanction (26(g)(3)). No privilege, protective-order motion or changed answer exists, so (b)(5)(A), (c)(1) and (e)(1)(A) do not apply.

cites.quote: A party may not seek discovery from any source before the parties have conferred as required by Rule 26(f)

Other parties have no duty to act on an unsigned disclosure, request, response, or objection until it is signed, and the court must strike it unless a signature is promptly supplied after the omission is called to the attorney's or party's attention.

If a certification violates this rule without substantial justification, the court, on motion or on its own, must impose an appropriate sanction on the signer, the party on whose behalf the signer was acting, or both.

stem: Pike serves a Rule 34 request on Dow Co. Dow serves no response by the due date. The next day Pike's lawyer files a motion to compel without contacting Dow's lawyer. Two weeks later, while the motion is pending, Dow produces everything requested. Dow offers no justification for its delay.
ask: Must the court order Dow to pay Pike's expenses of making the motion?

options.t: No; Pike filed before attempting in good faith to obtain the response without court action.
options.why: Rule 37(a)(5)(A) mandates expenses even when discovery is provided after the motion, but not if the movant filed before attempting in good faith to obtain it, 37(a)(5)(A)(i).

options.t: Yes; discovery provided after the motion was filed makes expenses mandatory with no exceptions.
options.why: Ignores the three exceptions in Rule 37(a)(5)(A)(i)-(iii), including a premature motion.

options.t: No; Dow's production moots the motion and ends the court's power to award expenses.
options.why: Rule 37(a)(5)(A) expressly covers the case where discovery 'is provided after the motion was filed.'

options.t: Yes, unless Dow shows that its lawyer, not Dow, caused the delay.
options.why: Adds an exception the rule lacks; the rule reaches the party or the attorney advising the conduct, and the listed exceptions are the only ones.

explain: Under Rule 37(a)(5)(A), if discovery is provided after a motion to compel is filed, the court must ordinarily require the party whose conduct necessitated the motion to pay the movant's reasonable expenses. But it must not do so if the movant filed the motion before attempting in good faith to get the discovery without court action. Pike never contacted Dow, so no award.

cites.quote: If the motion is granted—or if the disclosure or requested discovery is provided after the motion was filed—the court must, after giving an opportunity to be heard, require the party or deponent whose conduct necessitated the motion
the movant filed the motion before attempting in good faith to obtain the disclosure or discovery without court action

stem: Tarn moves to compel Orbit Inc. to answer four interrogatories after conferring with Orbit in good faith. Orbit's objections to two of them were unjustified, and its objections to the other two were upheld. The court grants the motion in part and denies it in part.
ask: What may the court do about the expenses of the motion?

options.t: It must order Orbit to pay all of Tarn's expenses because the motion was granted in part.
options.why: That is the mandatory rule for a motion granted in full under Rule 37(a)(5)(A); a split ruling falls under (a)(5)(C).

options.t: It must order each side to bear its own expenses, with no apportionment allowed.
options.why: Rule 37(a)(5)(C) authorizes apportionment and contains no each-side-bears-its-own mandate.

options.t: It must apportion the expenses equally between Tarn and Orbit.
options.why: Rule 37(a)(5)(C) is permissive ('may') and does not prescribe an equal split.

options.t: It may apportion the reasonable expenses after giving the parties a chance to be heard.
options.why: Rule 37(a)(5)(C) covers a motion granted in part and denied in part and says the court 'may' apportion expenses after an opportunity to be heard.

explain: A motion granted in part and denied in part falls under Rule 37(a)(5)(C), not the mandatory expense rules for a motion granted in full (A) or denied in full (B). The court may issue protective orders and may, after giving an opportunity to be heard, apportion the reasonable expenses for the motion. Neither full shifting nor equal division is required.

cites.quote: If the motion is granted in part and denied in part, the court may issue any protective order authorized under Rule 26(c) and may, after giving an opportunity to be heard, apportion the reasonable expenses for the motion.

stem: Hart sues Lee in federal court in State A. The parties stipulate that the deposition of Moss, a nonparty, will be taken by video, with Moss answering from her office in State B while all counsel sit in State A. At the deposition, Moss refuses to answer a question about the contract. Hart wants an order compelling her to answer.
ask: Where must Hart's motion for that order be made?

options.t: In the court in State A, where the action is pending, as with any discovery motion.
options.why: That rule applies to a motion for an order to a party; Rule 37(a)(2) sends a nonparty motion to the court where the discovery is taken.

options.t: In either court, at Hart's election.
options.why: Rule 37(a)(2) sets one court for a nonparty motion; it gives no election.

options.t: In the State B court, because the deposition takes place where Moss answers.
options.why: Rule 37(a)(2) requires a motion for an order to a nonparty to be made where the discovery is taken, and Rule 30(b)(4) places a remote deposition where the deponent answers.

options.t: In the court in State B, but only after Moss has been held in contempt.
options.why: Rule 37(a)(2) imposes no contempt prerequisite; a motion to compel comes first.

explain: A motion for an order to a nonparty goes to the court where the discovery is or will be taken (Rule 37(a)(2)). For a remote deposition, Rule 30(b)(4) says the deposition takes place where the deponent answers. Moss answers in State B, so Hart must move in the State B court. A motion directed to a party would go to the court where the action is pending.

cites.quote: A motion for an order to a nonparty must be made in the court where the discovery is or will be taken.
For the purpose of this rule and Rules 28(a), 37(a)(2), and 37(b)(1), the deposition takes place where the deponent answers the questions.

stem: In a personal-injury action, the court orders Pierce, the plaintiff, to submit to a Rule 35 physical examination by a physician named in the order. Pierce refuses to attend. The court finds the refusal willful and has not yet imposed any sanction.
ask: Which response is within the court's power under Rule 37(b)(2)(A)?

options.t: Treat the refusal as contempt of court, as with any other disobeyed discovery order.
options.why: Rule 37(b)(2)(A)(vii) permits contempt for any order 'except an order to submit to a physical or mental examination.'

options.t: Prohibit Pierce from introducing evidence of the injury, but not treat the refusal as contempt.
options.why: Rule 37(b)(2)(A)(ii) allows an order barring evidence, while (vii) excludes an order to submit to a physical or mental examination from contempt treatment.

options.t: Order only payment of expenses, because the further orders apply only to orders under Rule 37(a).
options.why: Rule 37(b)(2)(A) covers orders to provide or permit discovery 'including an order under Rule 26(f), 35, or 37(a).'

options.t: Impose no sanction, because only a party's officer, director or managing agent can be sanctioned.
options.why: Rule 37(b)(2)(A) reaches 'a party' as well as its officer, director or managing agent.

explain: Rule 37(b)(2)(A) applies to a party's failure to obey an order to provide or permit discovery, expressly including a Rule 35 order. The court may bar Pierce from introducing designated matters in evidence under (ii), and may use other listed orders such as striking pleadings or dismissal. But subparagraph (vii) forbids treating as contempt the failure to obey an order to submit to an examination.

cites.quote: fails to obey an order to provide or permit discovery, including an order under Rule 26(f), 35, or 37(a), the court where the action is pending may issue further just orders
prohibiting the disobedient party from supporting or opposing designated claims or defenses, or from introducing designated matters in evidence
treating as contempt of court the failure to obey any order except an order to submit to a physical or mental examination

stem: Brandt sues Mako Corp. Brandt never identified Gil in its Rule 26(a)(1) disclosures or in any supplement. After discovery closes, Brandt files a summary-judgment declaration from Gil. ask: May the court consider Gil's declaration on the summary-judgment motion?

options.t: Yes; the bar applies only at trial, not on a motion.
options.why: Rule 37(c)(1) lists 'a motion, at a hearing, or at a trial.'

options.t: No; Rule 37(c)(1) bars Brandt from using Gil's evidence on the motion.
options.why: A party that fails to identify a witness as Rule 26(a) or (e) requires may not use the witness on a motion, at a hearing or at trial, unless substantially justified or harmless.

options.t: Yes; the bar applies only after Mako obtains an order compelling disclosure.

stem: Dray serves proper Rule 33 interrogatories and a Rule 34 request on Larch Co. Larch serves no answers, objections or written response and files no motion for a protective order, explaining only that it considered the requests objectionable. No court order has issued. Dray's lawyer telephones Larch's lawyer twice to try to get the responses before filing a motion.
ask: May the court impose sanctions on Larch?

options.t: Yes, on motion with a good-faith certification; the Rule 37(b)(2)(A)(i)-(vi) orders are available.
options.why: Rule 37(d)(1)(A)(ii) covers a total failure to respond with no order needed; 37(d)(1)(B) requires the certification, and 37(d)(3) allows those orders.

options.t: No; sanctions require violation of a court order under Rule 37(b).
options.why: Rule 37(d)(1)(A)(ii) independently authorizes sanctions for a failure to serve answers, objections or a written response.

options.t: No; Larch's belief that the requests were objectionable excuses its failure.
options.why: Rule 37(d)(2) says objectionability is no excuse unless a protective-order motion is pending, and none is.

options.t: Yes, but only an award of expenses, since without an order the Rule 37(b)(2)(A) orders are unavailable.
options.why: Rule 37(d)(3) makes the Rule 37(b)(2)(A)(i)-(vi) orders available for a Rule 37(d) failure.

stem: Pell sues Rho Inc. for harassment. After Pell's lawyer sends a preservation demand, Rho's IT manager neglects to suspend an automatic deletion setting, and Rho's employees' text messages about Pell are lost. They cannot be restored or replaced. The court finds that Rho failed to take reasonable steps to preserve them, that Pell is prejudiced, and that Rho did not act with intent to deprive Pell of the messages.
ask: What may the court do?

options.t: Instruct the jury to presume the messages were unfavorable to Rho, because Rho's failure and Pell's prejudice suffice.
options.why: Rule 37(e)(2)(B) requires a finding of intent to deprive, which the court did not make.

options.t: Enter a default judgment against Rho, because the loss was Rho's fault.
options.why: Default judgment under Rule 37(e)(2)(C) likewise requires intent to deprive.

options.t: Impose no remedy, because without intent to deprive Rule 37(e) allows none.
options.why: Rule 37(e)(1) separately permits curative measures on a finding of prejudice.

options.t: Order measures no greater than necessary to cure the prejudice to Pell.
options.why: Rule 37(e)(1) allows curative measures on a finding of prejudice; the harsher measures in (e)(2) need a finding of intent to deprive.

stem: Pike sues Bale Inc. During the case: (1) Bale's managing agent, properly noticed, fails to appear for his deposition, and no court order has addressed it; (2) Bale never disclosed under Rule 26(a)(1) a witness, Sol, whom it now plans to call at trial; (3) a flood destroys Bale's paper files, and no electronically stored information is involved; and (4) Bale denied a Rule 36 request, but Pike has not yet tried to prove the matter. The court has issued no discovery orders, and both sides took part in developing the Rule 26(f) plan.
ask: Which Rule 37 provisions are available to Pike on these facts? Select all that apply.

options.t: Rule 37(b)(2)(A)
options.why: That provision punishes violating a discovery order, and the court has issued none.

options.t: Rule 37(c)(1)
options.why: Bale failed to identify Sol as Rule 26(a) requires, so it may not use him at trial unless the failure was substantially justified or harmless.

options.t: Rule 37(c)(2)
options.why: Expenses for a failure to admit arise only if the requesting party later proves the matter, and Pike has not.
A party's managing agent who fails, after proper notice, to appear for his deposition permits sanctions on motion, with no order required.

options.t: Rule 37(e)
options.why: Rule 37(e) addresses lost electronically stored information, and only paper files were destroyed.

options.t: Rule 37(f)
options.why: Both sides participated in developing the discovery plan, so no failure to participate exists.

explain: Bale's undisclosed witness engages Rule 37(c)(1), and its managing agent's failure to appear after proper notice engages Rule 37(d)(1)(A)(i), which needs no prior order. Rule 37(b)(2)(A) needs a disobeyed order; 37(c)(2) needs Pike to prove the denied matter later; 37(e) covers only ESI; and 37(f) requires a failure to participate in framing the discovery plan.

cites.quote: If a party fails to provide information or identify a witness as required by Rule 26(a) or (e), the party is not allowed to use that information or witness to supply evidence on a motion, at a hearing, or at a trial
a party or a party's officer, director, or managing agent—or a person designated under Rule 30(b)(6) or 31(a)(4)—fails, after being served with proper notice, to appear for that person's deposition

stem: Cato serves interrogatories on Dune Co. Dune answers interrogatory 5 with a response that skirts the question. After a good-faith conference, Cato moves to compel. ask: Which provisions of Rule 37 apply to Cato's motion? Select all that apply.

options.t: Rule 37(a)(3)(B)(iii)
options.why: A party's failure to answer an interrogatory under Rule 33 supports a motion to compel an answer.

options.t: Rule 37(a)(4)
options.why: An evasive or incomplete answer is treated as a failure to answer.

options.t: Rule 37(a)(5)(A)
options.why: The motion was granted and no exception applies, so the court must require payment of Cato's reasonable expenses.

options.t: Rule 37(a)(5)(B)
options.why: That provision applies when the motion is denied, and this one was granted.

options.t: Rule 37(b)(2)(A)
options.why: That provision punishes disobeying an order, and Dune has not yet defied one.

options.t: Rule 37(d)(1)(A)(ii)
options.why: Dune served answers, so this is not a failure to serve any answers, objections or response.

explain: Dune's evasive answer is treated as a failure to answer (37(a)(4)), so Cato may move to compel under 37(a)(3)(B)(iii). a party fails to answer an interrogatory submitted under Rule 33

the court must, after giving an opportunity to be heard, require the party or deponent whose conduct necessitated the motion, the party or attorney advising that conduct, or both to pay the movant's reasonable expenses incurred in making the motion, including attorney's fees

stem: Quade sues Rook Co. Rook's lawyer ignores Quade's repeated calls to schedule the Rule 26(f) conference and refuses to contribute to the written plan, so Quade drafts it alone. Later the court orders Rook to produce its sales records within 14 days, and Rook's CEO, personally, ignores the order. All of Rook's other discovery obligations have been met, and no electronically stored information has been lost.
ask: Which provisions of Rule 37 apply to these events? Select all that apply.

options.t: Rule 37(a)(5)(B)
options.why: That provision applies when a motion to compel is denied, and no such motion was denied.

options.t: Rule 37(b)(2)(A)
options.why: Rook's CEO, an officer, failed to obey an order to provide discovery, so the court may issue further just orders.

options.t: Rule 37(c)(2)
options.why: No Rule 36 request went unadmitted, so there is nothing to prove or recover.

options.why: No electronically stored information was lost.

options.t: Rule 37(f)

No denied motion, Rule 36 request, missed deposition or lost ESI appears.

If a party or a party's officer, director, or managing agent—or a witness designated under Rule 30(b)(6) or 31(a)(4)—fails to obey an order to provide or permit discovery

stem: The scheduling order sets a discovery cutoff of June 1, 2026. Dow's interrogatories to Tarn Co. were due to be answered May 20. By a written stipulation, the parties give Tarn 60 more days, which runs past the cutoff. Neither side asks the court to approve the stipulation. Tarn later relies on the extension to withhold its answers.
ask: Is the stipulated extension effective without court approval?

options.t: Yes; Rule 29 lets the parties modify any discovery procedure by stipulation, with no role for the court.
options.why: Rule 29(b) makes an exception for extensions that would interfere with the time set for completing discovery.

options.t: Yes; court approval is needed only for stipulations that shorten a time.
options.why: Rule 29(b) requires approval for extensions that interfere with the discovery cutoff, not for shortening.

options.t: No; a stipulation that interferes with the discovery cutoff needs court approval.
options.why: Rule 29(b) requires court approval for an extension that would interfere with the discovery cutoff, a hearing date or trial.

options.t: No; the parties may never stipulate to change the 30-day answer period for interrogatories.
options.why: Rule 33(b)(2) says a shorter or longer time may be stipulated to under Rule 29.

explain: Rule 33(b)(2) lets the parties stipulate to a different time for answering interrogatories under Rule 29. But Rule 29(b) requires court approval of a stipulation extending the time for any form of discovery if it would interfere with the time set for completing discovery, for hearing a motion, or for trial. This extension passes the June 1 cutoff, so it needs approval.

cites.quote: a stipulation extending the time for any form of discovery must have court approval if it would interfere with the time set for completing discovery, for hearing a motion, or for trial

stem: Ford sues Kell Co. The parties stipulate that nonparty Orr's deposition will be taken before Ames, a notary who is a friend of both lawyers, in Ames's office, on two days' notice and 'in the manner specified.' The court has issued no order on the subject. At trial, Kell offers the deposition, and Ford objects that it was not taken before an officer under Rule 28(a)(1) or on reasonable notice.
ask: Is Ford's objection to how the deposition was taken sound?

options.t: Yes; every deposition must be taken before an officer authorized to administer oaths under Rule 28(a)(1).
options.why: Rule 28(a)(2) defines 'officer' to include a person designated by the parties under Rule 29(a).

options.t: Yes; a stipulation shortening the notice period is ineffective without court approval.
options.why: Rule 29(a) allows 'any notice'; the court-approval limit in Rule 29(b) concerns extending time and interfering with deadlines.

options.t: No; Rule 29(a) lets the parties stipulate to the person, time, place, notice and manner.
options.why: Rule 29(a) permits a deposition before any person, at any time or place, on any notice; Rule 28(a)(2) counts a person the parties designate under Rule 29(a) as an officer.

options.t: No, but only if the court approved the stipulation in advance.
options.why: Rule 29 requires no advance approval for a Rule 29(a) stipulation, which operates 'unless the court orders otherwise.'

explain: Rule 29(a) permits the parties, unless the court orders otherwise, to stipulate that a deposition be taken before any person, at any time or place, on any notice, and in the manner specified, and it may be used like any other deposition. stem: Aldo and Bera, co-plaintiffs, sue Kline Co. Aldo has taken six depositions of Kline employees and Bera has taken four, all by oral questions under Rule 30. Bera now gives notice of another oral deposition. Kline refuses to stipulate and objects that the notice requires leave of court. No order has altered the usual limits.
ask: What must Bera obtain to take the new deposition over Kline's objection?

options.t: Leave of court, which must be granted if consistent with Rule 26(b)(1) and (2).
options.why: The deposition would make more than 10 taken by the plaintiffs, so Rule 30(a)(2)(A)(i) requires leave, which the court must grant to the extent consistent with Rule 26(b)(1) and (2).

options.t: Nothing, because each plaintiff may take 10 depositions separately.
options.why: Rule 30(a)(2)(A)(i) counts depositions 'by the plaintiffs' together; six plus four plus one exceeds 10.

options.t: Leave of court, which may be granted only on a showing of exceptional circumstances.
options.why: Exceptional circumstances is the Rule 26(b)(4)(D) standard for non-testifying experts; Rule 30(a)(2) applies Rule 26(b)(1) and (2).

options.t: Nothing, unless Kline moves for a protective order; until then the notice stands.
options.why: Rule 30(a)(2)(A) places the leave requirement on the noticing party when the parties have not stipulated.

stem: Ross's lawyer deposes Tate, a nonparty witness, on Monday. Tate's own lawyer interrupts with long speaking objections, and the examination uses the full 7 hours allowed for the day. options.t: Yes; the 7 hours limits each session, so he may resume the next day.
options.why: Rule 30(d)(1) limits the deposition to 'one day of 7 hours' unless stipulated or ordered.

options.t: Yes; because Tate's lawyer delayed the examination, the limit is automatically extended.
options.why: Impeding the examination is a ground for the court to allow more time, not an automatic extension.

options.t: No, and the court has no power to allow more time.
options.why: Rule 30(d)(1) says the court must allow additional time consistent with Rule 26(b)(1) and (2) in these circumstances.

options.t: No; he needs a stipulation or an order, and more time must be allowed if needed.
options.why: Rule 30(d)(1) limits a deposition to one day of 7 hours unless stipulated or ordered, and requires the court to allow additional time when needed or when the examination was impeded.

explain: Under Rule 30(d)(1), unless stipulated or ordered, a deposition is limited to one day of 7 hours. The 7 hours are used, so continuing requires a stipulation or an order. stem: Pace serves a Rule 30(b)(6) notice on Rook Co. that describes with reasonable particularity the matters for examination about Rook's 2024 pricing. Rook designates Tate, a salaried sales manager who is not an officer, director or managing agent but consents to testify. Tate had no part in 2024 pricing, though Rook's files and finance staff hold the information. At the deposition he answers most questions, 'I don't know; I wasn't involved.'
ask: Which statement is correct?

options.t: Rook could designate only an officer, director or managing agent, so Tate's designation is invalid.

stem: Before any Rule 26(f) conference in a non-exempt action, Wynn wants to depose Gil, a nonparty witness who has told Wynn he is leaving the United States for good in two weeks. stem: Gray serves an interrogatory asking Moto Inc. for its total sales by month for five years. stem: Kent sues Lyle Co. for breach of contract. Kent wants Lyle's own purchase records and also records held by Jules Bank, which is not a party. No stipulation or court order bears on the methods Kent may use.

ask: May Mica refuse to produce the same electronically stored information in a second form?

options.why: Jett's physical condition is in controversy, so the court may order an examination.

options.t: Rule 35(a)(2)(A)
options.why: The order was made on motion for good cause and on notice, as required.
